title: The five questions I ask before signing off on any system design
excerpt: Design reviews are only useful if you know what you are looking for.
body:
Design reviews are only useful if you know what you are looking for. Over many years of reviewing designs — my own and others' — I have distilled my process into five questions that reliably surface the most consequential risks.

The five questions

1. What is the failure model? Not the happy path — the failure path. What happens when each external dependency is unavailable? How does the system degrade? Is degradation graceful or catastrophic?

2. What happens at 10x load? Most systems are designed for expected load. The interesting question is what breaks first when load exceeds expectations. If the answer is "everything at once," the design needs work.

3. How do you know it is working? What observability does the design include, and is it sufficient to diagnose a production incident at 2am without access to the engineer who wrote it?

4. What does rollback look like? For any change that modifies data schemas, event contracts, or external interfaces, what is the rollback strategy? If the answer is "it is irreversible," that needs to be a deliberate, understood choice — not an oversight.

5. Who needs to change their behaviour? Every system change has human implications — for operators, for dependent teams, for users. Understanding these implications before launch is much cheaper than discovering them after.
